corrections.was: Pushed proportions are shapes exaggerated on purpose, as in a cartoon look. The three figures share one body, and the red head grows from fourteen percent of the height, about realistic, to twenty-two, then thirty-three. For example, the termite soldier picture used as a reference for a Walker enemy draws the soldiers with big heads, a pushed, cartoon look rather than a real insect's proportions.
corrections.now: Pushed proportions are shapes exaggerated on purpose, as in a cartoon look. The three figures share one body, and the red head grows from fourteen percent of the height, about realistic, to twenty-two, then thirty-three. For example, a player character drawn with an oversized head and short legs reads as a cartoon on purpose, not as a realistic person.
corrections.why: The example said the termite soldier reference shows pushed, non-insect proportions; Chapter 2 says only 'three big-headed termite soldiers in a pixel-art style', which does not establish exaggeration (real termite soldiers are big-headed), so the unsupported Walker claim is replaced by a plain cartoon-proportion case.

corrections.was: A perspective constraint is a limit that comes from the player's view, first person, third person or top down. The view limit shuts thirteen more ideas, and eighteen stay open. For example, Walker is seen from the side, so the termite reference, which shows the creatures from above, does not fit a side-view level without a new drawing.
corrections.now: A perspective constraint is a limit that comes from the player's view, first person, third person or top down. The view limit shuts thirteen more ideas, and eighteen stay open. For example, Walker is seen from the side, so the termite reference, which shows the creatures from above, may not fit a side-view level without a new drawing.
corrections.why: Chapter 2 confirms the soldiers are 'seen from above, and the game is seen from the side', but lists 'whether a top-down creature belongs in a side-view level' under 'Not verified by anyone', so the narration may not assert that it does not fit.

corrections.was: Seven features of one character, ranked. Iconic elements are the few features that keep a character recognisable even when tiny on screen. In this made-up example a feature shows only if its thinnest side is three pixels. The pauldron, the shoulder armour, survives down to twenty-seven pixels, the sword and scarf to thirty-two, the buckle needs ninety-six. For example, if your hero is known by a red scarf, draw the scarf big enough to show when the hero is small, and let tiny buckles go.
corrections.now: Seven features of one character, ranked. Iconic elements are the few features that keep a character recognisable even when tiny on screen. In this made-up example a feature shows only if its thinnest side is at least three pixels. The pauldron, the shoulder armour, survives down to twenty-seven pixels, the sword and scarf to thirty-two, the buckle needs ninety-six. For example, if your hero is known by a red scarf, draw the scarf big enough to show when the hero is small, and let tiny buckles go.
corrections.why: The slide's rule is a minimum ('Rule: 3 px on the thinnest side'; step 3: 'below 3 px ... no longer reads'), so 'is three pixels' becomes 'is at least three pixels'.

bookend_corrections.was: A high-poly sculpt is baked onto the low-poly mesh the engine runs.
bookend_corrections.now: A high-poly sculpt's detail is baked onto the low-poly mesh the engine runs.
bookend_corrections.why: Baking transfers the sculpt's detail into an image on the low-poly mesh (slide 10 step 4: 'Sculpt detail stored as an image on the low-poly'), not the sculpt itself; the body beat said 'stores the sculpt's detail'.
